description: The Sikh belief in the oneness of humanity and complete equality of all people, including equality of women.
content_html:
One God, One Humanity

The Sikh belief in the oneness of humanity flows directly from Ik Onkar — the oneness of God. Because there is one God, and because God’s light (jot) is present in every human being regardless of caste, religion, gender or nationality, all people are of equal worth and dignity. This is not merely a social ideal in Sikh teaching; it is a theological truth.

When Guru Nanak emerged from the River Bein after three days in what Sikhs believe was a direct encounter with God, his first words were: “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.” This declaration was radical in its context. Sixteenth-century Punjab was a society stratified by caste, religious division and gender inequality. Guru Nanak proclaimed that God sees none of these divisions; all are equally the creation of the one God.

Key Fact

Guru Nanak’s declaration “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim” was a foundational statement of the equality of all people before God. He expressed this in practice by sitting and eating with people of all castes — a radical act in a deeply stratified society.

Equality in the Lives of the Gurus

The ten human Gurus embodied the principle of equality throughout their lives. Guru Nanak travelled widely across South Asia and beyond, sharing his message of the oneness of God and humanity with people of all backgrounds. He rejected the caste system and ate and conversed with those considered “untouchable” in the social hierarchy of his day. The institution of langar (the free communal meal, discussed in the Practices unit) was one of his most concrete expressions of equality: all who came to eat sat together on the ground, sharing the same food, regardless of rank or religion.

Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, took the expression of equality a decisive step further when he founded the Khalsa in 1699 at Vaisakhi. He called five people from different castes to step forward and offer their lives for their faith — the Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones). By choosing men from different castes and initiating them as equals, Guru Gobind Singh abolished caste hierarchy within the Khalsa. He also gave Sikh men the common name Singh (lion) and Sikh women the name Kaur (princess) — replacing caste-marking surnames with shared names of honour.

Complete Equality of Women

The equality of women with men is stated explicitly in the Guru Granth Sahib and was a central teaching of Guru Nanak. This is highly significant because it was proclaimed in a society in which women had very limited status. The Guru Granth Sahib asks why anyone should consider women inferior when it is women who give birth to the leaders, kings and prophets of the world.

In Sikh practice, this equality has concrete expressions. Women lead worship in the gurdwara, read from the Guru Granth Sahib (granthi), and take part in all aspects of religious life. There is no principle within Sikh teaching that restricts women from any religious role. Amritdhari (initiated) women receive the same initiation as men at Amrit Sanskar, take the name Kaur, and observe the five Ks.

In contemporary British Sikhism, women serve as granthis, sing kirtan (devotional hymns) and organise langar at gurdwaras such as the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall. The principle of equality is woven into everyday Sikh life, not just into theological statements.

Sikh teaching is unambiguous: the caste system is rejected. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that caste distinctions have no value before God. However, sociological research including studies by the Sikh Network UK has documented that some Sikh communities in Britain continue to observe informal caste distinctions in social and marriage practices. This is a tension between stated religious teaching and lived practice. For the purposes of the exam, students should note: the teaching of Sikhism is complete equality, including abolition of caste. Where practice diverges from teaching, this is seen by many Sikhs as a deviation from authentic Sikh values, not as a sanctioned tradition.

Equality in the Guru Granth Sahib

The equality of all people is encoded in the Guru Granth Sahib in a remarkable way. The scripture contains the writings not only of the Sikh Gurus but also of Muslim, Hindu and other composers from different castes and backgrounds — among them Kabir (a low-caste weaver), Sheikh Farid (a Muslim mystic) and Ravidas (a leatherworker considered among the lowest in caste hierarchy). By including their hymns alongside those of the Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib enacts the teaching it proclaims: all who seek God are equally worthy.

At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall — the largest gurdwara in Europe — the langar serves thousands of people every week, with no charge and no distinction of religion, class or background. Visitors of all faiths are welcome. This practice directly enacts the Sikh teaching of the oneness of humanity. The Network of Sikh Organisations (NSO) actively promotes Sikh values of equality and interfaith dialogue in British civic life, demonstrating that equality is a living commitment, not just a historical teaching.

Key Fact

Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699, choosing the first five members (Panj Pyare) from different castes. He gave all Sikh men the name Singh and all Sikh women the name Kaur — replacing caste-marking surnames to express that, before God, all Sikhs are equally lion-hearted and equally honoured.
exam_tip_html:
On the 6-mark Explain question about Sikh beliefs on equality, name two specific sources or examples: the Guru Granth Sahib (citing its teaching that all people share God’s light) and either Guru Nanak’s founding actions (eating with people of all castes, his declaration “There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim”) or Guru Gobind Singh’s founding of the Khalsa (choosing the Panj Pyare from different castes; giving Singh and Kaur as equal names). The mark scheme requires a named source — “the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that God’s light is in every person” is a valid source reference.

For the 12-mark Evaluate on whether “Sikhism teaches complete equality for all people,” remember to argue both sides: FOR (the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak’s actions, the Khalsa); AGAINST or complicating (the gap between teaching and some community practice around caste and marriage). A Mastering answer names the sub-traditions (sahajdhari and amritdhari) and reaches a justified conclusion. Without a conclusion, you cannot access the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Sikh belief in the oneness of humanity flows from Ik Onkar: because God is one, and God’s light is in every person, all people are of equal worth — regardless of caste, gender or religion.
  • Guru Nanak proclaimed equality in word and deed; Guru Gobind Singh enacted it through the Khalsa, choosing the Panj Pyare from different castes and giving all Sikhs equal names (Singh and Kaur).
  • The Guru Granth Sahib itself expresses equality by including the writings of poets from different castes and religious backgrounds, enacting the teaching that all who seek God are equally worthy.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Sikh teaching of 'Ik Onkar' as it relates to humanity?
A) All Sikhs are equal but others are not
B) God is present only within the Khalsa
C) All people share the same divine light and are equal before God
D) Equality applies only to men and women within Sikhism
practice_questions.marks: C) All people share the same divine light and are equal before God [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: What names did Guru Gobind Singh give to Sikh men and Sikh women when he founded the Khalsa?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for Singh (given to men); 1 mark for Kaur (given to women).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the belief in equality is expressed in Sikh teaching or practice.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- Guru Nanak ate and conversed with people of all castes, demonstrating that God sees no caste distinction — this means he enacted the teaching that all people are equal before God (1 + 1 marks).
- The Guru Granth Sahib includes the writings of poets from different castes and religious backgrounds (e.g. Kabir, Sheikh Farid, Ravidas) — this means equality is encoded into the scripture itself, not just stated in its words (1 + 1 marks).
- The Khalsa initiation admits members equally regardless of caste, and all receive the shared names Singh and Kaur, replacing caste-marking surnames (1 + 1 marks).

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the equality of women is important in Sikh teaching.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two developed reasons, each with a link to the Guru Granth Sahib or a specific action of the Gurus. Possible points: (1) The Guru Granth Sahib explicitly affirms women's worth — it asks why women should be considered inferior when they give birth to the leaders and teachers of the world; this means Sikh scripture itself challenges the gender inequality of its historical context. (2) Guru Gobind Singh admitted women to the Khalsa on equal terms to men, giving them the name Kaur and requiring them to observe the same five Ks — this means equality between men and women is expressed in the highest commitment within Sikhism.
Secure (3-4 marks): Reasons present, mostly accurate; source named but development limited.
Developing (1-2 marks): One reason, limited development, source absent.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
'The Sikh belief in equality is the most important Sikh teaching.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
- refer to Sikh teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Equality flows directly from Ik Onkar — God's oneness makes human equality a theological truth, not just a social ideal. Without this teaching, Sikhism's social vision would be lost.
- The Guru Granth Sahib's explicit rejection of caste and affirmation of women's equality were radical at the time of composition and remain foundational to Sikh identity.
- The Khalsa's founding expressed equality in the most public, visible way — choosing the Panj Pyare from different castes and giving all members equal names.
- In British Sikh communities, equality is expressed through langar and open gurdwaras, making it arguably the most visible Sikh teaching to non-Sikhs.

Arguments against:
- The belief in God's oneness (Ik Onkar) might be considered more fundamental, since it is the source from which equality flows — without monotheism, the equality argument has no theological foundation.
- Mukti and the spiritual journey (five khands) could be seen as the ultimate aim, with equality serving that aim rather than being primary in itself.
- Some Sikhs would argue that sewa (service) or the Guru Granth Sahib as living Guru are equally important teachings.

Mastering (10-12 marks): Both sides argued with Sikh sources; justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, mostly accurate, some sources, conclusion present.
Developing (4-6 marks): Mostly one-sided, limited sources.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Parveen is a Sikh woman who has recently moved to Birmingham and is attending her local gurdwara for the first time. She is surprised to see women reading from the Guru Granth Sahib during the service. Explain two reasons why this reflects Sikh teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. Students may include:
- Sikh teaching holds that men and women are completely equal before God — because God's light is in every person regardless of gender, there is no Sikh principle that restricts women from reading or leading worship (1 + 1 marks).
- The Guru Granth Sahib explicitly affirms women's worth and Guru Nanak taught against gender discrimination — the practice of women serving as granthi (reader) enacts the founding teaching of the faith (1 + 1 marks).

knowledge_checks.q: What was Guru Nanak's declaration after his encounter with God at the River Bein?
options: There is no king, there is no peasant
There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim
There is no man, there is no woman
God is one and the Guru is one

knowledge_checks.q: Which Sikh Guru founded the Khalsa in 1699?
The first five members of the Khalsa, drawn from different castes, are known as the _____ Pyare.
In Sikhism, the name given to all initiated women to replace caste-marking surnames is _____.
Match each example to the Sikh teaching on equality it expresses:
right: Equality across religion and social class
Abolition of caste hierarchy in the Khalsa
Complete equality of women with men

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Sikh belief in the 'oneness of humanity' mean?
flashcard_questions.a: All people share God's divine light and are of equal worth before God, regardless of caste or gender.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Guru Nanak's declaration after three days in the River Bein?
flashcard_questions.a: There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim — proclaiming the equality of all before God.
The Five Beloved Ones — the first members of the Khalsa, chosen from different castes by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.

flashcard_questions.q: What names did Guru Gobind Singh give to Sikh men and women?
flashcard_questions.a: Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women, replacing caste-marking surnames.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Guru Granth Sahib express equality through its content?
flashcard_questions.a: It includes hymns by poets of different castes and faiths, such as Kabir (weaver) and Sheikh Farid (Muslim mystic).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Sikh principle regarding women's roles in worship?
flashcard_questions.a: Women are fully equal to men and may serve as granthi (reader), lead worship and take part in all religious roles.
The Sikh who reads from the Guru Granth Sahib during worship — any Sikh, male or female, may serve in this role.

flashcard_questions.q: How does langar express the Sikh belief in equality?
flashcard_questions.a: It is a free communal meal open to all people regardless of faith, caste or background — enacting equality in daily life.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Sikhism teach about the caste system?
flashcard_questions.a: The caste system is rejected — caste distinctions have no value before God, as the Guru Granth Sahib teaches.

glossary_terms.definition: The Sikh teaching that all people share the same divine light and are therefore of equal worth before God.
The Five Beloved Ones — the first members of the Khalsa, chosen from different castes by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699.
The name given by Guru Gobind Singh to all initiated Sikh men, meaning 'lion', replacing caste-marking surnames.
The name given by Guru Gobind Singh to all initiated Sikh women, meaning 'princess', expressing their equal honour.
The person who reads from the Guru Granth Sahib during Sikh worship — any Sikh, male or female, may take this role.
The tenth and final human Guru of Sikhism (1666-1708), who founded the Khalsa in 1699 at Vaisakhi.

hero_image_caption: Sikh teaching proclaims the oneness of humanity — all people share God's divine light and are equal before Waheguru.
